That has been exacerbated because of the attack and the apparent dislocation of the seaport of Massawa and the cut-off of the main supply lines, particularly for the churches to fulfil the obligations that the Archbishop of Canterbury announced a couple of weeks ago.

February 16, 1990
Oral Questions
Since the government's special representative, the Senior Vice-President of CIDA, Mr. Doug Lindores, has just returned home, can the minister indicate what special measures we can take to assure Canadians that all of their efforts to meet the famine threat again in Ethiopia will be satisfactorily met?
Second, because it now appears more than ever that conflict is the ultimate cause of this recurring famine situation, what measures would Canada take in concert with others to try to find peace where it is very much needed in the Horn of Africa?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are very concerned about the impact of conflict upon people already struck by famine. The Port of Massawa is to all intents and purposes now closed. We have diverted a ship bound for that port with food and supplies from Canada to Port Sudan where there is a better prospect of getting that cargo delivered.
The hon. member is correct in identifying the source of the problem to be the conflict. We have delivered the strongest possible requests to the governments of both Ethiopia and Sudan, and indirectly to rebel leaders, urging them to go back to negotiation.
We are working with all of the international organizations involved in delivering emergency assistance and co-ordinating it, trying to find some way to deliver help in the context of conflict.
Obviously, what has to happen is an agreement by all sides for a cease fire, an agreement to return to negotiation. We are using every means open to us to urge that course upon all parties.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
According to the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council disparity between Atlantic Canada and the rest of the country is growing at an unprecedented rate. The Atlantic fisheries has been mismanaged into a state of utter collapse.
According to the Tourism Industry Association of Nova Scotia the new 7 per cent goods and services tax will devastate the tourism industry in Atlantic Canada.
Yet with the full knowledge that our regional economies are the last to recover from but the first to slip into a recession, this government has recklessly pursued a high interest and high dollar policy.
Will the minister now finally admit that he has lost complete control and credibility and step aside before he causes a complete collapse of the fragile Atlantic Canadian economy?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate what the hon. member said, that people in the country today are apprehensive about what might happen in the economy. That is understandable in view of what has happened in recent years. I refer to the recession of 1981-82. There is no one calling for a recession of that order of magnitude.
There is still a balance of opinion today. Some say we may be heading for a recession, some say we are not heading for a recession, but clearly we are in a period of slow growth.
The reason this is necessary is to allow us to get inflation out of the economy. That inflation is affecting the economy of Atlantic Canada as it is affecting other parts of the country. I would say to my hon. friend that if we let the problem of inflation get out of control in the country it will have a more profound effect on the economies of the Atlantic provinces because they do not have the same economic strength as southwestern Ontario, for example, would have to withstand that pressure.
That is why we must deal with that. At the same time as we do that we have allowed for an increase in funding for Atlantic Canada, through the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency-
You are joking.

My hon. friend says that we are joking. The level of funding in Atlantic Canada, I believe, is 35 per cent in this five-year period relative to the first five years of our mandate. A 35 per cent increase is an increase, even with the arithmetic that my hon. friend wants to use.

Mr. Speaker, a few more answers like that from the Minister of Finance and they will be guaranteeing that not one Conservative candidate in Atlantic Canada gets their deposit back after the next federal election.
February 16, 1990

My supplementary question is to the same minister. Yesterday the Conference Board of Canada predicted an economic stormfront for Atlantic Canada. The minister should know that his fiscal policies, coupled with this government's mismanagement of the fishery, has pushed Atlantic Canada to the brink of a full-blown recession.
What action is this minister prepared to take to ensure that his policy of high interest rates is not the final nail in the coffin of the fragile economy of Atlantic Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend does not do justice to the strength of the economy in Atlantic Canada today. We acknowledge there is a serious problem with the Atlantic fishery, but there are other parts of the economy in Atlantic Canada which are not suffering as is the case with the fishery.
I made it quite clear as far back as the April, 1989 budget that we must deal with the problem of inflation. If we do not deal with the problem of inflation the people in Atlantic Canada will be more severely hurt than other parts of the economy, such as southwestern Ontario, that are stronger. That is why we must do that.
But there is an offset here in the increase in the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency funding. There is an increase of funding there that will help offset the impact of higher interest rates and that is how we are dealing with the problems as it relates to Atlantic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. The Ottawa-Carleton business community has finally given up trying to reason with this government to get direct non-stop air service to Chicago. This is the nation's capital, the fourth-largest region in the country, and the only major city in Canada denied direct services to customers and markets through Chicago.
When a major carrier is ready to provide this service four times a day, when the business community needs it, why is the minister saying no?

Mr. Speaker, I am sensitive to the request by the Ottawa-Carleton corporation but there is a problem. My hon. friend knows very well that the routes between the United States and Canada are controlled by a bilateral agreement. If we make a decision to re-open the bilateral agreement we have to consider not only Ottawa. We have requests from Edmonton and Halifax for other routes and those requests will have to be dealt with at the same time.

Pearson International Airport is a mess with near misses in the air up by 64 per cent. It will not cost the government one red cent to let Ottawa travellers by-pass Pearson and also to help local businesses compete internationally to bring tourism and conventions to the nation's capital.
Why is the government protecting private airlines from competition in this new free market? Why is it putting its interest ahead of a dynamic business community and safety at Pearson?

Mr. Speaker, I do not see the relationship between the first and second questions. I hope there is not.
First, Pearson is not a mess. Since December, 1989, there has been a cap on flights at Pearson. With 20 million passengers a year I think my colleague will understand that it is different to manage Pearson than it is any other airport in the country. Pearson is safe.

Second, I will repeat what I said before. To reopen the bilateral agreement with the United States is something which cannot be done only with Ottawa. I understand that the hon. member serves Ottawa. However, I have to

February 16, 1990

serve Halifax and Edmonton, too. This is the way it should be done. I will not reopen the bilateral agreement just for Ottawa. I am sorry, but it cannot be done.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the senior minister from Atlantic Canada, the Minister for International Trade.
My colleague and I have just got back from visiting fishing communities in Newfoundland and heard firsthand about the crisis in Atlantic Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce that today in Paris a debt rescheduling agreement was concluded between the representive of the Government of Poland and the representatives of the Paris Club of official creditors, including Canada.
While, we do not have all the details yet, I understand that the agreement reached will reschedule Polish payment obligations due during 1989-90 and the first quarter of 1991.
Under this agreement, Canada expects to reschedule 100 per cent of the payments of principal and interest due during this period totalling more than $1.2 billion. This represents approximately 10 per cent of the $12.2 billion total rescheduled by all Paris Club creditors.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to raise an item of business under the heading of "Motions" which I believe will commend itself to the House.
Routine Proceedings
As hon. members may know, Mr. Jean-Marc Hamel will cease to hold office as Chief Electoral Officer on Monday, February 19, 1990.
The Canada Elections Act requires that the Chief Electoral Officer be appointed by resolution adopted by the House of Commons.
There has been consultation with the Opposition and I believe you will find unanimous agreement to the appointment of Mr. Jean-Pierre Kingsley as Chief Electoral Officer.
Therefore, I am pleased to move the following resolution:
WHEREAS Mr. Jean-Marc Hamel will cease to hold office as Chief Electoral Officer on February 19, 1990;
AND WHEREAS subsection 6(2) of the Canada Elections Act, Chapter E-2 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1985, provides that in the event of a vacancy in the office of the Chief Electoral Officer, the vacancy shall be filled by resolution of the House of Commons;
BE IT therefore, resolved that Mr. Jean-Pierre Kingsley is hereby appointed Chief Electoral Officer effective February 19, 1990.
Mr. Speaker, if I may, I would like to break with tradition at this point and suggest that because of the importance of this particular resolution, and that Mr. Kingsley will become an officer of Parliament, the motion be seconded by the member for Thunder Bay- Atikokan and the member for Kingston and the Islands in order to indicate that there is unanimous agreement and that all three parties concur in this particular motion.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to put on the record a few words regarding the new appointee, Mr. Jean-Pierre Kingsley.

Jean-Pierre Kingsley is a graduate of the University of Ottawa. He has held several positions in the Public Service and the private sector. From 1977 to 1981, Mr. Kingsley was President and Chief Executive Officer of the Ottawa General Hospital. From 1981 to 1984, he was Assistant Deputy Minister in the Department of State for Social Development. Later, he was Deputy Secretary of the Personnel Policy Branch at Treasury Board, until 1987.
]English]
That, Mr. Speaker, is the area where I had the pleasure of working with Mr. Kingsley, who I see in the gallery today. I want to say personally that this is a very

February 16, 1990
Routine Proceedings
fine public servant who will do the position of Chief Electoral Officer and the country proud.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Canada is fortunate to have this great administrator as Chief Electoral Officer.

I also want to place on the record a word of appreciation for the retiring Chief Electoral Officer. For some 24 years, Mr. Jean-Marc Hamel has been the Chief Electoral Officer of Canada. He undertook those responsibilities on June 6, 1966, and was responsible for the administration of the act during the last seven general elections, since 1968.
Mr. Hamel has always undertaken his work with a thorough understanding of the basic requirements of the position. I am quite sure that many hon. members here who have had the opportunity to come into contact with Mr. Hamel will agree that he possessed the fairness and the impartiality that has been traditional in this office and which is greatly desired and indeed necessary in the proper administration of the functions of the office.
I am sure all members will agree that Canada has been well served by Mr. Jean-Marc Hamel during his tenure as Chief Electoral Officer.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion that the Minister of Justice has placed before the House is one that I am very happy to support on behalf of the members of the official opposition in this House.
I am also pleased to say that we are delighted with the appointment that the Minister of Justice has proposed.

Mr. Kingsley is without doubt a very distinguished Canadian public servant. His career has been remarkable and we are very proud to have him as Chief Electoral Officer of Canada.

We look forward to working closely with Mr. Kingsley in his new office. We hope that we will establish with him the normal lines of communication that are so important
between the political parties of Canada and the Chief Electoral Officer.
Speaking personally as the election critic in our party, I have worked with Mr. Hamel, and I look forward to working with Mr. Kingsley in the same way.
I must also say that on behalf of the opposition that Mr. Hamel has performed an outstanding service for Canada as Chief Electoral Officer for the last 24 years. In the short time that I have been able to work with him, I have found his knowledge of his office outstanding, his knowledge of the electoral law of Canada outstanding, and his ability to work with members from all parties outstanding.
I reflect the views of all hon. members when I say that he has been an outstanding public servant and an outstanding officer of Parliament, which, of course, is what the Chief Electoral Officer is.
The unusual part about today's appointment is the fact that this position is appointed by a resolution of this House. The position of the Auditor General of Canada and this position may be the only two appointments made by resolution of the House of Commons.
The fact that we are able to agree on an appointment of this kind is an indication of the co-operation that exists between all parties, and also because of the outstanding qualities that the new office holder has which have commended him to all members of this House.
I thank you for the opportunity to second this particular motion, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I also want to say a few words, both about the new appointee, Mr. Jean-Pierre Kingsley and the outstanding Mr. Jean-Marc Hamel.
Over the last couple of days, I had the privilege of working on behalf of my leader in the consultations to reach this point today, working in a fashion that we should do more of, particularly when it comes to either by statute or by process that we consult for these kind of appointments.
Mr. Jean-Marc Hamel is an individual who has developed a great amount of respect within my party over the 24 years of his service. We have had any number of senior members of the party who have worked directly with him both during and between elections, and they ah
February 16, 1990

speak very highly of his approach to a very, very difficult job.
We thank him for those years of service and wish him well. We hope he appears before the Royal Commission to pass on his final thoughts as a private citizen as opposed to the Chief Electoral Officer. However, we do wish him well and I know he will find that there is life after elections, as all of us find out sooner or later.
I am pleased to second, on behalf of my party, the resolution appointing Mr. Jean-Pierre Kingsley as Chief Electoral Officer. We learned through our consultation process of his vast experience in the public sector, both in terms of government and the voluntary sector such as hospitals. In consultation with my colleague, the member for Nickel Belt, who has had occasion to sit across the table with Mr. Kingsley on matters dealing with conflict of interest, his most previous post, he indicates that Mr. Kingsley is extremely fair, straightforward and comes to the point. That is the type of individual we need in this office. It is a very delicate office. One could ask why Mr. Kingsley would even want the job, given the nature of it, but we look forward to working with him. Perhaps he may not be here for 24 years, but neither will some of us.
I congratulate Mr. Kingsley on what will almost immediately be his appointment after we pass this resolution. I and members of my party look forward to working with him in the years to come.

Mr. Speaker, I will not prolong this, but I just want to endorse all the remarks that were made, especially by my House Leader, as well as those made by the spokesman for the official opposition and my friend, the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan.
Having shared with Mr. Hamel almost the 20 some years that he has held that position, and I do not want to go through all the elections we have shared together, but I just want to endorse, in a very personal way, all of the constructive comments that were made.
Jean-Marc Hamel, whom I got to know in those seven elections he held office, is the personification to me of the type of public servant this country has been blessed with. He had duality in both languages and he also shared duality in the practical problems of a politician along with the problems of interpreting the Canada
Routine Proceedings
Elections Act. In those few times during a campaign one had to phone the Chief Electoral Officer, whether it was Jean-Marc Hamel or someone in his office, the information came back and it really helped in those difficult times. As the deadline for the election day got closer and the tenseness thereby of the campaign got a little more heated, there was always the calmness and the common-sense of this office.
I wanted to say-and this may save me from writing a letter to Jean-Marc Hamel-these few words of encouragement for his tremendous service to the country, and for Jean-Pierre Kingsley, who I do not know as well but know about, I certainly hope that in his days as he gets initiated into this most fascinating world that he will obviously consult from time to time with Jean-Marc Hamel to see how you go about discharging such an important duty that affects us all in this land.

Mr. Speaker, like my colleague from Kingston and the Islands (Mr. Milliken), I would like to support the appointment of Jean-Pierre Kingsley. I know Mr. Kingsley; he is a dedicated, honest, down-to-earth man who is devoted to the community. I knew him on the board of directors of the Montfort Hospital in the region. I know that Jean-Pierre Kingsley will be an excellent Chief Electoral Officer for Canada.
I must also thank Jean-Marc Hamel for his work. I ran in only one federal election under Mr. Hamel and I hope to have the opportunity to run in many under the very capable direction of my friend Jean-Pierre Kingsley. Congratulations and bravo!

-again and again, election after election, with no problems and no complaints from members of Parliament.

The House resumed consideration of the motion Mr. Clark (Yellowhead) that Bill C-25, an act to amend the Geneva Convention Act, the National Defence Act and the Trade-marks Act, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak to Bill C-25, at third reading stage, and have an opportunity to express a few views and opinions on this whole matter of the Geneva Protocols. In 1977, in Geneva, two protocols to the 1949 Geneva Conventions

February 16, 1990
Government Orders
were achieved. Bill C-25 simply seeks to ratify the two protocols and to codify them in Canadian statute law.
In a general sense no one would object to the Geneva Protocols. However, I do have some reservations on some aspects of them. First of all I would like to talk about the general impact that such protocols have. The Geneva Conventions referred to law applicable in time of armed conflict, humanitarian law or rules of conduct in war. The protocol served to broaden the scope of the Conventions. For instance, they include additional protection for prisoners-of-war and rules regarding children in armed conflict.
In addition, the Geneva Conventions Act is amended so that its language is consistent with that of the protocols. The National Defence Act is amended so that there are no statutory limitations on the prosecution of serious breaches, again consistent with the protocols. Moreover, the amendment to the Trade Marks Act introduces legal protection for the new international distinctive sign for civil defence.
In the past, the Geneva Protocols and the Geneva Conventions were drawn up and adopted by various international governments, primarily in the western world, largely as a result of the slaughter that took place in World War I, in western and eastern Europe. It was an attempt to set forth rules and regulations and, indeed, laws of an international nature with respect to the treatment of combatants, both on the battlefield and upon being taken prisoner-of-war. Certain decent humanitarian provisions were set forth whereby prisoners of war, combatants in uniform, would be treated with decency and respect, not as a defeated mob but as soldiers, sailors, airmen, officers and other ranks. They would be treated according to a protocol that was already set forth in the various militaries prior to their going to war and prior to their being captured.
There is a certain amount of irony. This is one of the points I want to make. There is a certain amount of rather bitter irony attached to the Geneva protocols. What the protocols say is simply this: If you volunteer or if you are drafted and you go to war and you shoot and kill because you may be killed in return, you attempt to destroy your enemy, his munitions and his supply, total war, in other words, and if you are captured in doing so, coming out of a rather uncivilized, almost dehumanizing experience, and put into a prisoner of war camp, then
you have to be treated in a certain civilized way. You have to be provided with clean, warm bedding, with meals that are nutritious, and to be treated in such a way that you are not tortured, hurt or harmed and you do not endure any physical or mental pain. If you are an officer, under no circumstances are you to be billeted with the other ranks. That was simply a throw-back to the class system that was prevalent in Europe in the 1920s. It was a reflection of the nineteenth century. There is a bitter irony here.
The protocols said that after you engaged in war, destruction and death, pillage and carnage and the destruction of all kinds of property of a military and non-military nature, you were to be treated with common decency. Moreover, if you were an officer, you were to be treated even better. You were to have better accommodations. You were not to be forced to do manual labour. But if you were a captured officer, you could, under orders from those who held you prisoner, order your other ranks, the privates, the corporals, the sergeants and so on, to do manual labour.
While this is extremely ironic, I am not arguing that prisoners of war should not be treated humanely. Of course they should. What I am saying is that while the protocols lay down certain rules of decency for combatants, we have no laws nor international conventions as to the treatment of innocent civilians. We bomb their homes, we bomb the factories, we flood the mines when the workers are in them. I read enough about World War II to make me as sick as anybody else. The allies who sent their bombers out day after day and night after night over Germany and other occupied countries in Europe for what they called precision bombing. When they discovered that we were no good at precision bombing and that, given the technology we had at that time, precision bombing was virtually impossible, we changed its name to saturation bombing. That way the bombardiers did not have to worry about hitting the target; a 1,000 planes instead of 100 were sent to wipe out whole sections of cities. Both sides indulged in this kind of carnage.
While we spent a lot of time in the 1920s drawing up the Geneva Protocols as to the treatment of combatants taken prisoner, we totally ignored those who suffer the most in war-the innocent, the elderly and the children. We still do. The ultimate desecration of humanity in the name of war and victory was the dropping of the atomic bomb in Hiroshima in August, 1945. We were not satisfied with the block-busters wiping out whole blocks of innocent people. We were not satisfied with saturation
February 16, 1990

bombing that wiped out whole sections of cities. We had to go to total destruction with the atomic bomb at Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
As we ponder this afternoon-and we will be supporting this legislation-humanizing the behaviour of combatants with respect to children and extending this treatment to combatants involved in civil insurrections and civil wars as this bill does, we should pause and think about how we can put into force international law with respect to the treatment of the innocent during times of conflagration. We should be spending far more time in attempting to bring about the end of war itself and building up statutory law of an international nature that would prevent or act as a severe sanction against any nation state precipitating a war. That is the thrust of our thinking.
I was very pleased to be a very small part of the Open Skies Conference this week. I had a chance to spend some hours at the conference centre. I congratulate the government for sponsoring this conference. Today, men and women of good will are coming together, both east and west, in an attempt to work out differences and put in place various protocols that will build confidence and establish a lasting peaceful order in Europe. A lot more has to be done in terms of the Third World and other flash points on the globe.
This legislation should be looked upon in a broader sense but also in another sense. We and the government have come out strongly in favour of extending the protocols to revolutionary movements, civil insurrection, where groups are fighting for democracy, freedom, and so on. But by the same token we find it very difficult to become involved in, or critics of, various incidents and events that are going on around the world that are contrary to peace, stability and the furtherance of democracy and liberty. I have several in mind but one would be the whole question of El Salvador.
I know that our Secretary of State for External Affairs has a different view with respect to El Salvador than does his counterpart in Washington. I am not trying for a
Government Orders
moment to link the government with Washington on the El Salvador issue. But I honestly do not think that our government is doing enough to drive home to President Bush that the number one reason for fighting, killing and destruction in El Salvador today is the financial aid given by the United States to the Salvadoran government. If that financial aid were withdrawn tomorrow that entire struggle would come to an end in very short order. We are not doing and saying enough. We are not publicizing the wretchedness of the Cristiani government.
President Bush looks upon President Cristiani of El Salvador as that "beacon of light and hope", I think he called him, "for democracy in Latin America". Just a few weeks ago I had the privilege of listening to a young lady by the name of Miss Ridd in my constituency on a Saturday night who described to me the horrors of the justice system in El Salvador. Anybody who is thought to be working against the interests of that awful government of Cristiani is arrested and thrown into jail. One of the most popular kinds of torture in that country is to put a gunny sack around a suspect's head; tie it at the neck but before doing so throw in a handful of lime; and then beat the person so that when they hyperventilate and breathe in the lime, it bums their lungs. It is only a matter of months before they expire after they have been released. That is the beacon of hope for democracy in Central America that Mr. Bush refers to, the ARENA administration under President Cristiani.
So, I call upon our government to be more forceful and public in its condemnation of that regime.
Another area where we have totally walked away from protocol and international law and turned a blind eye was the American invasion of Panama. With the information we have, one can only conclude that former General Noriega is involved in illicit drug traffic. Obviously, he is a thoroughly disreputable individual and he should have been captured, arrested and brought to trial, et cetera. But just because an international criminal of great infamy is at large in a country does not lend any credibility or justification to the United States-a country that purports to be a democracy-to invade that country with military force to overthrow its head of state.
We have international police forces, international law, custom, jurisprudence, rules and regulations and proto-

Government Orders
cols to deal with that in a civilized way. Yet, it is little wonder that the President of the United States ordered that invasion. He had read the polls and had been told that he had a sort of wimp image and that he had to get tough. He had to present himself to the public as a Rambo and that is why it was done. Within a day or two polls were taken and some 80 per cent of the American people backed him. And this government backed him. That is what I find despicable at this moment. Without any reservation the Government of Canada stated that it was regrettable but it supported the President of the United States and his invasion of Panama.
There are other places where we are not doing enough to bring into focus and observation assaults against democracy, liberty and human rights. I refer, of course, to East Timor. Despite the UN Charter's recognition of the right of a people to self-determination, the Canadian government refuses to recognize this right in practice when it comes to the case of East Timor.
East Timor is occupied by the Indonesian government following an invasion in the late 1970s. Canada has accepted the occupation and even engaged in efforts to have the issue removed from the UN human rights agenda. That is not acceptable. If we really believe in decency and humanity in international protocols, if we really believe that we have to treat people in a humane, decent and fair manner in time of war, civil insurrection and civil war, then we have to be consistent and support human rights and civil liberties throughout the world regardless of political ideology.
I can refer also to the situation in Romania as it existed before the violent overthrow of the Causcescu regime. We have been involved in that country for a number of years with respect to the construction of a Candu reactor. Surely, there must have been some Canadians attached to that project who were aware of the wretched, inhumane working conditions by which the Romanian people had to labour. It was nothing short of slave labour camps, working on starvation diets. Our hands are not clean. If we did not know, we should have known. When we found out, as I suspect we did months before, we should have cancelled the project at that moment and dismantled what we had done rather than adding more to that wretched inhumanity to the slave labour workers by continuing to construct the CANDU reactor.
There are many other examples of human rights being denied and Canada doing very little about it. I will refer finally, and there are many others, to the West Bank and Gaza-to the Middle East. As I have said on many occasions in this House the problems of the Middle East will not be addressed and peace will not come to that tortured part of the world until the Palestinian cause is addressed and settled. I do not care what has been argued and said in the past by members of all parties, the fundamental fact remains that the Palestinian people have been denied a homeland. They have been denied that homeland for over 40 years. It is their land, their buildings, their farms, their orange groves.
It is rather interesting that the State of Israel today can say, "The reunification of Germany is up to Germans. As long as they promise to be democratic, law-abiding it is not going to be a bad thing, it is not going to hurt us." I agree with that argument. But when it comes to re-establishing a homeland for the Palestinians, when it comes to Palestinian rights, human rights and liberties, somehow Israel cannot apply the same measure of honesty and decency. With wave after wave of Soviet Jews now emigrating from the Soviet Union, no doubt for many good reasons, and going to the Middle East, going to Israel, this powder keg is going to blow up. There is no other way of putting it.
Why is the Canadian government not taking a more active role? I know the Secretary of State for External Affairs has come out as a much stronger defender of the Palestinians and the Palestinian cause than any of his predecessors. I congratulate him for his courage. But I call upon this government, that if it really truly believes in the protocols that are going to be passed into statutory law later today through third reading vote that it also adopt the same humanitarian approach to all of these other examples where human rights are being violated, whether it is in El Salvador, Panama, East Timor or as they were in Romania and as they have been for 40 years in the West Bank and Gaza.
I want conclude by simply saying, yes, we will accept this third reading. We will support Bill C-25. But I hope that this government will expand its thinking and will expand its work in the field of human rights bringing a sense of humanity to international protocols and bringing justice to down-trodden people such as the Palestinians in their valiant struggle to establish and re-establish for themselves their homeland. So we in the New Democratic Party support Bill C-25 at third reading
February 16, 1990

and I suspect that it will be given that third reading in due course this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support Bill C-25, an Act to amend the Geneva Conventions Act. I want to address my comments on this important bill. It governs the laws applicable in time of armed conflict and it serves to include the additional protections for prisoners of war and the rules regarding children in armed conflict. This is to be applauded although as my hon. colleague has pointed out that being the last decade in this century it seems somehow anachronistic that we are still making rules to govern behaviour in time of war.
There are a number of wars going on in the world currently. These protocols are expanded to the rules not only in international conflicts but to cover civil wars. When I was in Africa, in Eritrea, in 1986, during a civil war, there was no UN observation of the prisoners of war in the region in which I was travelling. Fortunately, I can report to the House that the 10,000 prisoners of war in an open camp, helped by the Eritrean Peoples Liberation Front, were being fairly treated in spite of the aerial bombardment of their former comrades in the Ethiopian air force. The Eritrean people managed to tiy to keep them safe in spite of the ongoing war. The extension of these conventions to include victims of civil war is an important amendment that should be applauded.
I want, in my address this afternoon, to pursue two themes regarding Bill C-25. The Canadian government supports international conventions, and this particular international convention, but there is an inconsistency here with the application to those conventions that Canada has already signed. Previous speakers have addressed a number of examples. I would just like to reiterate a few as well as add a couple.
Second, while working not only to develop rules of conduct for wartime, we should be putting additional resources into the prevention of wars. I have some suggestions on how that can proceed.
Government Orders
Let me turn to my first theme, namely, that there is an inconsistency of Canadian government policy with regard to the application and respect for international conventions.
As this House knows, I travelled to El Salvador last spring during that country's elections. Subsequent to that the ARENA government came to power and we have seen massive violations of human rights under the ARENA government. We have seen the bombing of the civilian population which is in absolute disregard of the UN declaration.
As we have seen on our television screens, there is the kind of mistreatment or lack of treatment accorded to FMT .N fighters in the city of San Salvador, where they refused treatment to those wounded in wartime. Yet Canadian silence has encouraged the ARENA government. If there are these international protocols, why do we not speak out more forcefully when they are violated so blatantly as the ARENA government in El Salvador has done?
We cannot do more than pay lip service to these conventions. It is all very well but the signing of them means something more than a just a piece of paper. We have a responsibility to make sure that they are respected.
Then there is the issue of Panama. The Canadian government's support for the American invasion of Panama, I think, has received the kind of reaction from the Canadian media and the Canadian people that it deserved, that it was a direct contravention of the international principles of national sovereignty. This kind of excuse that the Canadian government has given that, "Oh, this was a special case, and that we have to make sure that the Americans are supported in this very special case", is absolutely utter nonsense. If there are international conventions we have to respect them and there are can be no special cases for the violation of national sovereignty. We are talking about the kind of chipping away at what the United Nations is about by that kind of support for such blatant American expansionism as I would like to term it.
There is another example of ignoring an international body's rulings-and I would like to expand on that-and

February 16, 1990
that is the whole issue of asbestos. Canada has ignored international labour organizations restrictions on the sale and use of asbestos. We are selling tonnes of it to Thailand. I think this kind of contradiction of international convention is most despicable. When we sign a convention we have to live up to its terms; that is why we sign it. The tripartite agency of the United Nations had been concerned with the hazards of asbestos in the early 1970s.
Canada regarded a number of the proposed provisions of the code of practice of the United Nations dealing with this issue as serious threats to the asbestos industry.
Canada undertook a world-wide embassy by embassy diplomatic offensive in Third World and East Bloc countries. Most of these governments guaranteed that all the delegates sent to Geneva would be pro-asbestos. This is not an inconsistency; it is an outright contradiction to what Canada said they were for. Despite this concerted action to defeat the International Labour Organization's recommendation, the UN convention did pass narrowly.
In another little side bar to all of this, Canada which normally rails against South Africa's blue asbestos came to its aid saying it should not be there because it was irreplaceable. This convention on asbestos was to try to obtain substitutes. It did narrowly pass. As soon as it did, Canada being a signatory opened a disinformation campaign to try to lessen its effects. This is shameful behaviour of a supposedly responsible, well developed western nation. Canada blatantly ignored clear International Labour Organization directives and put together a sophisticated marketing package. It now fully intends to offset its dwindling sales of asbestos in western Europe and North America by turning to the underdeveloped countries of the Third World for markets.
This is the kind of outright contradiction to international conventions that is totally unacceptable. If we are signing these things we have to be able to respect them. We have to stand as an example that it is not just a piece of paper, that it has to be respected.
I point out that we are in favour of signing these conventions. The conventions on conduct are important examples and symbolic gestures during the time of war. Because it now extends it to prisoners of war in civil
Government Orders
wars, there is a recognition that the kinds of wars which are sometimes the most brutal are those that are not international in nature but are civil. There are national liberation fronts which are also worthy of our concern to ensure that the rules of war are respected.
I am told that the Americans are having second thoughts about ratifying the protocols which we are speaking about this afternoon for that reason. They have some concern about respecting prisoners of wars of national liberation movements and giving them a recognized status. Canada's ratification of this bill this afternoon will be an important symbolic gesture that Canada sees the importance of addressing the concerns of prisoners of war of national liberation fronts.
My second theme is about the whole situation of preventing wars. We have the rules for conduct of war, but we have to give resources now to preventing wars to make them an obsolete form of conflict resolution. There is a number of ways that we can do that. First, we have to improve the resources to the United Nations. The United Nations is an international body that has always been zapped of resources and has been trying to play the peacekeeping role, the conflict resolution role and all such things with very limited resources.
We have seen the kinds of examples when it does work such as in Namibia, which gives us great hope that this is the kind of expanded role the United Nations can play.
We also know that Canada has allocated its armed forces to take place in the peacekeeping observation role in Central America. This is something that should be applauded. These are where our resources are. It is a good investment. It is an investment in peace. Not just an expansion of the United Nations role is necessary, we have to ensure a more equitable distribution of the world's resources.
As a member of the subcommittee on international debt, I am acutely aware of the kind of conflicts that result because of poverty. That is something we as Canadian citizens have to be concerned about. It does affect us. Those conflicts in El Salvador, those conflicts that I have witnessed in Africa and Eritrea, affect us because those people are at war. It is not just the horrible human costs, but it is threatening to us; international security is threatened when there are conflicts.

The House resumed from Monday, December 4,1989, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-34, an act to establish the Canadian Centre for Management Development and to amend certain acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying back on December 4 when I started to speak on this bill, I have to judge it in the context of what I believe the role of the Public Service of Canada is and whether this is or is not supportive of that role.
I was saying that no program we mandate or fund in this House is delivered without the Public Service employees of Canada. They are our eyes and ears on the front line of service to the public, feeding back to us, if we are wise enough to listen, the changing needs of Canadians and the world we live in. The role of the Public Service and how best to support the further development of competence, excellence, creativity and commitment to the nation and to service to the public depends on how one views the role of government. There is a huge myth that if only government worked like the private sector, God would be in Heaven and all would be right with the world.
There is a very clear and different role for the two sectors. The bottom line of the private sector is profit and the bottom line of the public sector is service to people and to the future of Canada. Both have to operate efficiently and effectively but each has a different reason for existing. That means they exist and operate in different ways.

Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada is the biggest employer in this country. There are one-quarter of a million public servants working directly for Canadians. Another quarter million work in Crown corporations and more or less independent but federally regulated government agencies.

This, in my view, gives the Parliament of Canada tremendous responsibility to ensure that government leads by example, to be on the cutting edge of new

February 16, 1990
Government Orders
approaches to developing the most important resource any nation has the talent and the ability of its people. The people resource becomes even more important as we head toward an economy where 70 per cent of the economic activity will not be in resource development and manufacturing but in services and information. Who should know better than government the ethic of service and the importance of information to the setting of future direction.

The workplace faces many challenges. Technological change requires us to consider human resources in a new light and realize that young people will no longer be schooled and trained in the expectation that for the rest of their lives, they will have a relatively stable occupation. It is essential to provide for on-going renewal of workers' skills if we are to avoid constant disruption of people's personal and professional lives.
It will be extremely important to have a good idea of employees' abilities so as to maximize their development. We must get rid of our prejudices about who is the best equiped to exercise a given profession and about the value of work which, for many years, was evaluated according to the social groups that were traditionally responsible for certain tasks.

If justice and fairness and equity were not compelling enough reasons, making the best possible use of every bit of talent this nation possesses requires that old biases and barriers be stripped away. The government must ensure that minorities, women, disabled persons and aboriginal peoples are given an equal opportunity at employment and advancement in the Public Service.
The workplace of the future will require flexibility to change. Old ideas about hierarchy and top-down management, every old concept about organizations and reporting structures will need to be re-examined. The pace of change will be too fast to rely on the old models of reorganizing massive structures to respond to new needs. Working relationships will need to become more important than reporting relationships, or the structures in which they operate.

On big issues like the environment, the old procedure of determining who is responsible and who is liable and who must make decisions will just not work. New relationships will have to be established in a spirit of partnership between decision-makers, managers and workers. The government must show the way in this regard.

I have examined the milieu of the Public Service and I have been struck by the lack of any cohesiveness in setting policy and direction for the most important tool of government. The Public Service is responsible for advising on policy, for delivering services and for managing the fiscal and physical resources of the people of Canada. I am amazed that there is no committee of this House that routinely calls to account the Treasury Board, the Privy Council Office and the Public Service Commission for their management of a work force of 250,000 people, 10 per cent of the national expenditures.

It is distressing to note that the right-wing policy of contracting out, privatizing and dismantling government institutions, the means by which public policy is carried out, is being applied without any consideration of its effects on the professionalism and dedication of the Public Service, on the quality of public services, on the protection of public health and safety and on the costs of government.

People are being hurt in the process. Careers are being interrupted in mid-stream. Staffs have been downsized to the point of exhaustion, families are being devastated to the point of instability and uncertainty about their future. Whole communities are being decimated. Morale is down, people are stagnating in their careers, the Public Service is aging, its international reputation for excellence is being lost. Yet, there is no mechanism for holding the government accountable for its actions.
That is the context in which I examine the bill. Will it improve accountability for the functioning of the Public Service? Will it better prepare the Public Service to meet the challenges of the future with creativity, competence and optimism? Will it reinforce or damage the commitment of the Public Service to the future of the nation
February 16, 1990

and to service to Canadians? Will the centre encourage the partnership of all employees in achieving those objectives?

Will it help or hinder the development of the talents of all those who work for the people of Canada? Will it help all public servants, regardless of their sex, colour, ethnic origin or handicap, give their best or prevent them from doing so? Will it better prepare the Government of Canada to show initiative and set an example of enlightened human resource management?

There is a desperate need for revitalization of the public sector for restoring pride and commitment to service to the public, and for restoring confidence that the importance of one's work is understood and valued. That has been seriously undermined in recent years. The rebuilding needs to be a joint effort, drawing on the knowledge, experience and dedication of all Public Service employees. Yet, I have serious concerns about the potential for the Centre for Management and Development to further isolate management from the shop floor, so to speak.
I have some serious concerns that the bill and the centre itself isolates management from the very sources of renewal, the people on the front lines, in the labs, out there serving the people of Canada from coast to coast.
The management structure of the centre ensures that only the upper echelons will have any say in how the centre functions, how management functions and ultimately how the Public Service functions. It further isolates management from accountability to Parliament and, therefore, to the people of Canada by concentrating power, control and decision-making in the Privy Council Office.
It has the potential, if it is not properly structured, to further block entrance to management by groups that have traditionally been excluded, to set up an exclusive management cadre of people who belong to the same clubs, went to the same schools, go to the same dinners and live in the same neighbourhoods. That is not what the Public Service of Canada needs. It makes no provi-
Govemment Orders
sion for linking management training with training throughout the Public Service.
The legislative committee on Bill C-34 and Parliament will have a unique opportunity to examine the results of the bill before it is passed because the centre has been operating for over a year. It will have the obligation on behalf of the people of Canada to find out why a budget of $4.5 million for executive training has jumped to an extravagant $11.5 million for this centre. It will have to take the time to find out whether this expenditure is improving the management and functioning of the Public Service of Canada or only preserving the turf of the management category.
I am happy to support this bill in principle. I think an initiative is needed. I look forward to a legislative committee where some needed amendments to the bill will be introduced to overcome some of these problems I have mentioned and to make sure the bill accomplishes its mission. This is no time for luxurious, over-funded, self-serving elitist institutions. It is time to get down to the hard work of preparing the Public Service of Canada at all levels to meet the challenges of the future with creativity, daring and innovation. It is time to win the confidence of every employee and to reinforce their ability to contribute to the building of a nation which has just begun.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to support Bill C-34, an Act to establish the Canadian Centre for Management Development and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof.

The legislation establishes the Canadian Centre for Management Development as a departmental corporation focusing on the training, orientation and development of senior managers in the federal Public Service. The centre will also conduct research into issues directly
related to public sector management and develop teaching materials related to its mandate.
The bill will retain the features of the previous bill, C-148, but establishes the centre as a departmental corporation rather than as a department. As a department corporation the centre will come under the direction of a board of governors composed of chief executive officers from the private sector, senior members of the Canadian academic community and deputy heads of the federal government departments.

Mr. Speaker, I would now like to pay tribute to John L. Manion, the first "Principal" of the Centre.

Mr. Manion, the first principal of the Canadian Centre for Management Development served in various functions in the Public Service for the past 37 years. As a dedicated public servant he deferred his retirement to set up this centre. His dedication included his love of helping others and of training people. He served 10 years in Manpower and 15 years in Immigration to rise to the position of Deputy Minister. It is a rare occasion indeed when a deputy minister rises from within staff. In 1979 he moved to Treasury Board before moving on to the Privy Council as senior personnel advisor. It was very fitting that John Manion be appointed as the first principal of the Canadian Centre for Management Development.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add that Mr. Manion was named an Officer of the Order of Canada in 1984 and that he received the Public Service Outstanding Achievement Award in 1986. Moreover, in 1989, the Public Administration Institute of Canada awarded him the Vanier Medal in recognition of outstanding achievements and special leadership in public administration in Canada.
I would also like to pay tribute to the person who I think first had the idea of a Canadian centre for management development, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier.
It was the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier who, in 1974, had the original idea. On October 31, 1977, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier introduced Bill C-304 in the House. He is the one who proposed this initiative.
February 16, 1990

In 1977, my colleague moved two motions in the House for discussions of this matter, one on May 6, and the other on October 31, 1977.
In 1981, he moved a new motion which was debated in the House. Finally, in 1987, he once again had a motion put on the Order Paper to establish a national school of government administration.
On behalf of my colleagues in the Liberal Party, I wish to express once again our support for this initiative to establish a Canadian Centre for Management Development, an initiative that was first brought before this House by a Liberal member, the member for Ottawa- Vanier, in 1974.
The centre replaces the former Centre for Executive Development in Tourraine operated by the Public Service Commission. The 1989-90 estimates for the operation of the centre are $9.6 million compared to $4.5 million in 1988-89. The centre is operating both at Tourraine and in the de La Salle Academy building on Sussex Drive.
Bill C-34 is a revised version of Bill C-148, and proposes that the CCMD be established as a departmental corporation with a board of governors rather than a department and an advisory council. The mandate of the centre includes the orientation, training and development of senior management in the federal public service and in the public sector, as well as in research into improved public sector administration.
Through training, orientation and development, the centre is designed to ensure that the senior public service managers improve the analytical, creative, advisory, administrative and other managerial skills and knowledge necessary to develop policy, to respond to change and manage government programs and services efficiently and effectively.
The centre will focus on attracting high-calibre candidates to the public service. It will conduct research into theory and practice of public sector management. The bill will also provide for co-operation between the centre and other institutions involved in management development and for the delivery of programs outside the public service.
Government Orders
The objects empowered to the centre are as follows: To encourage pride in the management of Public Service and to foster among Public Service managers a sense of purpose, values and traditions of the Public Service;
to help ensure that managers in the Public Service have the analytical, creative, advisory and administrative and other managerial skills and knowledge necessary to develop policy, respond to change and manage government programs and services efficiently and effectively;
to encourage and facilitate, through its programs and studies, the attraction of persons of high calibre to the Public Service, and to support their growth and development as public sector managers committed to the service of Canada;
to develop and provide training, orientation and development programs for managers in the public sector and particularly for senior managers in the Public Service;
to study and conduct research in the theory and practice of public sector management; and
to encourage a greater awareness in Canada of issues related to the public sector management and the process of governance and to involve a broad range of individuals and institutions in the centre's pursuit of excellence in public administration.

We agree with the objects of the Centre for Management Development, which includes the object to help ensure that managers in the Public Service have the analytical, creative, advisory, administrative and other managerial skills and knowledge necessary to develop policy, respond to change and manage government programs and services efficiently and effectively.
We agree with its object to attract through its programs and studies persons of high calibre to the Public Service, and to support their growth and development as public sector managers committed to the service of Canada.
We agree with its object to formulate and provide training, orientation and development program for managers in the public sector and particularly for senior managers in the Public Service.

February 16, 1990
Government Orders
We could not agree more that we need a centre that will develop management skills, and improve the productivity of public sector employees and the quality of services offered to Canadians.
However, a number of reservations were expressed by my colleagues from the Liberal caucus. One of my colleagues from the other place was concerned that the government would be competing directly with the universities and their public administration programs. I share his concern, but I am confident that academics on the board of directors will ensure that the centre complements courses offered by various Canadian universities but does not try to take their place. Briefly, the centre will offer a wide range of courses, seminars, conferences and development workshops for managers. To do so, it will need many case studies as well as a wealth of documentation, most of which does not exist at this time, either in the public sector or our universities.
Other colleagues were concerned about hiring procedures, powers and accountability of the board of directors, and the need to ensure the centre remains sensitive to the needs of the public service. Finally, there were concerns that the centre would become an elite club for senior executives. I must admit I share some of these concerns, since there is no mention of ways of increasing the number of Francophones at senior levels or of providing for equitable representation of women, visible minorities, aboriginal people and the disabled. However, my greatest concern would be to see a stagnating public service.
I would like to mention the Corporate Management Strategy, as presented by the Canadian Center for Management Development. On the title page we see the theme:

"Excellence in thought and and action to overcome today's problems and to meet tomorrow's challenges".
The Statement of Mission and Vision is extremely admirable:
The mission of the Canadian Centre for Management Development is to strengthen the management capacity of the public sector, and particularly of the senior levels of the federal public service, with a view to improving the quality of government and enhancing the service to the people of Canada.
This mission will be accomplished, in full co-operation with Canada's best in the public, private, and academic sectors, by extending the frontiers of knowledge in the practice of public sector management and by developing in public servants the knowledge, values, and skills critical to overcoming current and future management challenges.

In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to emphasize that I am delighted the centre will take up residence in the historic Academie de La Salle building, located in the National Capital Region. I hope the University of Ottawa will also be involved. This location witnessed the earliest beginnings of the University of Ottawa, at the turn of the century. Several years ago, the federal government renovated the premises, and it has given us a building that makes us proud of our heritage. The architecture was well preserved throughout the renovation of a building that was originally a French Canadian institution.
The University of Ottawa was founded at the turn of the century, and I myself had the honour and the privilege of graduating from the university in the 50s, with a master's in administration, majoring in education.

I hope the centre will be open and accessible to both public and private interests, includng MPs and their staffs, to promote understanding of government. The centre will be a benefit to small government agencies and scientific establishments that previously had no place for developing and fine tuning management skills.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-34, an act to establish the Canadian Centre for Management Development and to
Government Orders
amend certain acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to stand here and speak on Bill C-34, an act to establish the Canadian Centre for Management Development and to amend certain acts in consequence thereof.
In 1977, my esteemed colleague, the member for Ottawa-Vanier, proposed, as a Private Members' Bill, the establishment of, in his words, "a sort of College Canada for the administration echelons of the Government of Canada whereby the excellent reputation of the Canadian Public Service known throughout the world would be honed, polished and made even more ready to serve not only the federal government but all of the people of Canada".
The bill tabled, which would have established such a centre, died on the Order Paper at the end of that Parliament.
On April 15, 1988, Bill C-148 was first introduced to Parliament. The bill, which received unanimous approval by the House of Commons on August 25,1988, proposed to establish the Canadian Centre for Management Development. Unfortunately, the thirty-third Parliament was dissolved before the bill was sent back to the House for final approval. Therefore, Bill C-148, too, died on the Order Paper.
Legislation has once again been introduced in the House of Commons that would establish this centre. The bill is a revised version of Bill C-148 and proposes that the Canadian centre be established as a departmental corporation with a board of governors rather than a department with an advisory council.
This latter fact brings up an interesting point, one that came up during the space agency centre discussions. The revised proposal would have a board of governors rather than a department with an advisory council. Whenever this happens, the fundamental issue becomes whether this type of structure undermines the accountability of the centre to the government and to Parliament.
Furthermore, the responsibilities of the proposed board of governors are not clearly defined in this bill and thus raises many questions that should be thoroughly studied. For example, what kind of power will the board be given? The principal is an ex officio voting member of the board. Does this mean that the principal can, at the

February 16, 1990
Private Members' Business
same time, report to and be accountable to the board of which he or she is a member?
Because there are no selection requirements, can the governors be selected without due regard to equitable representation of women, visible minorities, aboriginal people and persons with disabilities? There is no limit of renewal of appointments to the board by the Order in Council. Could this not lead to the institutions becoming more insular and self-perpetuating?
I am very pleased that the proposal for the idea that the member for Ottawa-Vanier made over 10 years ago looks as if it may actually have time to possibly work its way through the system. The establishment of such a centre would provide for the orientation, training and development of senior managements in the federal Public Service and the public sector, as well as research into improved public sector administration.
The establishment of the centre goes a long way to correcting some of the problems in the Public Service that were pointed out by the Auditor General this past October. In his report the Auditor General said that the management of Canada's Public Service needs a new and creative outlook, one not concerned with vicious slashes, but rather a better management. The future holds new challenges and the Public Service needs to adapt to these challenges.
Through training, orientation and development the centre will be designed to ensure that senior Public Service managers improve the analytical, creative, advisory, administrative and other managerial skills and knowledge ncessary to develop policy, respond to change and manage government programs and services efficiently and effectively.
If this is to work, it is essential that we study whether the goal of the centre is to adequately prepare persons throughout the Public Service for management, including meeting employment equity objectives, and reflect adequately how management affects excellence, pride and Public Service attitudes at all levels.
I found it interesting to note that nowhere in Clause 4, which is where the objects of the centre are discussed, is there any reference to promoting the equitable representation in management of women, visible minorities, native persons and persons with disabilities. Nor does the clause refer at all to the relationship of management with employees at all levels or to the responsibility of the centre and the management category to encourage
pride, excellence and service to Canada and Canadians by all Public Service employees. It is this excellence, pride and service that the Auditor General was referring to in his report.
In conclusion, the discussion of this bill is long overdue and I am very pleased to be speaking on it. The creation of this centre will go a long way in helping our public servants maintain that excellence. The creation of the centre would enable the Public Service to recruit and maintain highly qualified individuals. At the same time the centre would enable the Public Service to address some of the problems outlined in the Auditor General's report.
The Public Service is an essential part of the functioning of this nation. I am proud to represent a riding where there are many, many public servants. All too often this government forgets or misunderstands just how important the Public Service is. The creation of the Canadian Centre for Management Development would allow the Public Service the support it requires in order for its efforts to be more effective in maintaining that excellence.
